neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Tongue: bilateral atrophy, fasciculations prominent at rest. Dysarthria present. Palatal elevation bilaterally reduced. Jaw jerk very brisk.
neurological_exam.motor: Bilateral arm weakness: deltoids 3+/5, biceps 4/5, hand intrinsic muscles 3/5. Bilateral thenar and hypothenar wasting. Fasciculations visible bilateral arms. Lower extremities: mildly weak hip flexors 4+/5, bilateral calf atrophy.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 4+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 4+. Knee jerks 4+ bilaterally. Ankle jerks 3+. Bilateral Hoffmans. Bilateral Babinski signs.
neurological_exam.additional: Classic ALS examination: tongue atrophy+fasciculations (LMN bulbar) + brisk jaw jerk (UMN bulbar) + bilateral Babinski (UMN) + arm wasting+fasciculations (LMN) + brisk reflexes (UMN) = combined UMN+LMN.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive weakness, tongue twitching, and speech difficulty over 12 months
patient.history_present_illness:
Mr. N is a 60-year-old retired teacher with a 12-month progressive history of bilateral arm and leg weakness, tongue fasciculations, dysarthria, and bilateral hand wasting. The presentation is a classic, straightforward case of ALS. He first noticed left hand weakness and wasting approximately 12 months ago. Over the following months, his right hand became similarly affected. He has had visible tongue twitching for 8 months and his speech has become slurred and strained. He has episodic uncontrollable laughing and crying. He has bilateral calf atrophy and a stiff, spastic gait. His wife has observed progressive decline in all motor functions.

On examination, all the cardinal features of ALS are present: tongue atrophy and fasciculations (lower motor neuron bulbar), jaw jerk brisk and bilateral Babinski (upper motor neuron), bilateral arm and leg weakness with wasting and fasciculations (lower motor neuron), and brisk hyperreflexia (upper motor neuron). Sensory examination is completely normal. This constellation of combined UMN and LMN features in a 60-year-old man without a compelling alternative diagnosis is definite ALS pending confirmatory workup.

findings.location: Bilateral corticospinal tracts from motor cortex to brainstem

signal_characteristics.T2: Low T2 signal band — iron deposition

mri.impression: 1. Bilateral symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of the corticospinal tracts from motor cortex to brainstem. 2. Low T2 signal band at the bilateral primary motor cortex, consistent with iron deposition. 3. No mass, hemorrhage, or demyelinating lesions. Borderline frontal volume loss. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.finding: Tongue: fibrillations +3, fasciculation potentials (complex, high amplitude). Severely reduced recruitment.

Bilateral FDI, APB, deltoids: fibrillations +3, PSWs +3, fasciculation potentials complex. Large amplitude (8-12 mV) long duration polyphasic MUPs. Severely reduced recruitment. Cervical paraspinals bilateral: fibrillations +2.
Bilateral TA, gastrocnemius, vastus medialis: fibrillations +2, fasciculations, large MUPs. Paraspinals: fibrillations +1.
All sensory NCS entirely normal bilaterally.
Severely reduced CMAP amplitudes all tested muscles. Normal conduction velocities. No conduction block.

quantitative_data.classification: Clinically definite ALS by Awaji and El Escorial criteria

specialized_test.impression: Widespread severe active denervation (fibrillations +2–+3, positive sharp waves) and chronic reinnervation (large amplitude polyphasic MUPs, severely reduced recruitment) in bulbar, cervical, thoracic, and lumbosacral regions — four body regions affected. Sensory NCS entirely normal bilaterally. Severely reduced CMAP amplitudes with normal conduction velocities; no conduction block. Findings indicate a widespread disorder of lower anterior horn cells. Clinical correlation required.

output.impression: Oropharyngeal dysphagia with silent aspiration of thin liquids (PAS score 6). Puree consistency tolerated with chin-tuck compensation. Residue in bilateral pyriform sinuses. Recommend thickened liquids (honey consistency) and mechanical soft diet. Speech-language pathology follow-up recommended.

critical_actions: NIV initiation indicated — SNIP 38 cmH2O is below threshold of 40 cmH2O
PEG tube planning — must be placed before FVC falls below 50%
Initiate riluzole — survival benefit in ALS
Swallowing evaluation — silent aspiration confirmed; diet modification prevents aspiration pneumonia
Advance care planning — advanced ALS with rapid decline rate requires early discussion
contraindicated_actions: Delaying NIV — SNIP below threshold; delay worsens hypercapnia and quality of life
Waiting until FVC <50% for PEG — PEG is technically safer and has better outcomes when placed at FVC 50-70%
key_reasoning_points: This is a straightforward textbook ALS presentation: classic UMN+LMN combination with tongue fasciculations (highly specific for ALS), brisk reflexes in wasted muscles (paradoxical), bilateral Babinski, normal sensory NCS
NIV threshold: SNIP <40 cmH2O in symptomatic ALS indicates NIV should be started promptly — survival benefit demonstrated
PEG timing is critical: placed when FVC is 50-70% (safe anesthesia); if delayed until FVC <50%, procedural risk increases substantially
CK 1240 U/L reflects extensive ongoing denervation — higher CK in ALS correlates with more active disease

metadata.notes: Classic straightforward ALS. Textbook presentation with all cardinal features. NIV immediately indicated given SNIP below threshold. PEG planning critical timing.
